---
title: "Categorical and Bernoulli distributions"
execute:

A corpus annotation can record a label, such as an interrogative lemma, or a binary property, such as whether the token is an object. These outcomes require two closely related distributions: the [**categorical distribution**](https://mc-stan.org/docs/functions-reference/categorical-distribution.html) for a finite label inventory and the [**Bernoulli distribution**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html) for a binary indicator.

We begin with the token-level annotation table, model the full lemma inventory categorically, and then collapse the relation label to a Bernoulli indicator while tracking what information that collapse removes.

## Turkish interrogative arguments

We use [UD Turkish BOUN 2.18](https://universaldependencies.org/treebanks/tr_boun/), a Turkic treebank built from five written registers of the Turkish National Corpus. Türk et al. ([2022](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10579-021-09558-0)) describe the sampling and native-speaker annotation, while Marşan et al. ([2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.11782)) document later agglutination-sensitive revisions. The release is CC BY-SA 4.0. The teaching extract retains tokens whose lemma is *hangi* ‘which’, *kim* ‘who’, or *ne* ‘what’ and whose source dependency relation is `nsubj` or `obj`; it does not infer unannotated dependencies.

One row is one annotated token. Tokens remain nested in sentences, and the selected registers are not a probability sample of Turkish usage. Thus the empirical probabilities below describe this pinned corpus extract.

```{r}
#| label: load-ud-categorical
library(ggplot2)

questions <- read.csv(
  "data/ud-turkish-boun/question-core-arguments.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

lemma_counts <- as.data.frame(table(questions$lemma), responseName = "count")
names(lemma_counts)[1] <- "lemma"
lemma_counts$probability <- lemma_counts$count / sum(lemma_counts$count)

relation_counts <- as.data.frame(
  table(questions$dependency_relation), responseName = "count"
)
names(relation_counts)[1] <- "relation"
relation_counts$probability <- relation_counts$count / sum(relation_counts$count)

stopifnot(
  nrow(questions) == 167L,
  setequal(lemma_counts$lemma, c("hangi", "kim", "ne")),
  abs(sum(lemma_counts$probability) - 1) < 1e-12,
  all(questions$object == as.integer(questions$dependency_relation == "obj"))
)

lemma_counts
relation_counts
```

The first source row is the *kim* subject token displayed in the [canonical
Turkish dossier](../foundations/possibilities-and-events.qmd#outcomes-and-the-sample-space).
Its categorical lemma value is *kim*. Recoding its relation answers a distinct
binary question: `nsubj` becomes `object = 0`, while an `obj` row becomes
`object = 1`. Zero here is a linguistic alternative, not missingness.

## Categorical outcomes

Let $L$ record interrogative lemma and let $\mathcal L$ be its finite support. A categorical probability vector $\boldsymbol\pi=(\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_K)$ satisfies $\pi_k\geq0$ and $\sum_k\pi_k=1$. We write

$$
L\sim\operatorname{Categorical}(\boldsymbol\pi),
\qquad
p_L(\ell_k)=\mathbb{P}(L=\ell_k)=\pi_k.
$$

The maximum-likelihood categorical probabilities are the empirical relative frequencies,

$$
\widehat\pi_k=\frac{n_k}{n}.
$$

To derive this result, the categorical log likelihood is
$\ell(\boldsymbol\pi)=\sum_k n_k\log\pi_k$ with
$\sum_k\pi_k=1$. Adding a Lagrange multiplier gives
$n_k/\pi_k=\lambda$ for every $k$. Summing
$\pi_k=n_k/\lambda$ over categories yields $\lambda=n$, and thus
$\widehat\pi_k=n_k/n$.

The extract contains `r nrow(questions)` tokens. Its most frequent lemma is *`r lemma_counts$lemma[which.max(lemma_counts$count)]`*, with empirical mass `r sprintf("%.3f", max(lemma_counts$probability))`.

## Binary outcomes

Define $O=1$ when the source relation is `obj` and $O=0$ when it is `nsubj`. Then

$$
O\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p),
\qquad
\mathbb{P}(O=o)=p^o(1-p)^{1-o},\quad o\in\{0,1\}.
$$

The fitted value is $\widehat p=n^{-1}\sum_i o_i$, computed here as `r sprintf("%.3f", mean(questions$object))`. This is a corpus proportion, not an estimate from independent sentence sampling.

The Bernoulli log likelihood is
$\ell(p)=(\sum_i o_i)\log p+(n-\sum_i o_i)\log(1-p)$. Setting its derivative to
zero gives $\widehat p=(\sum_i o_i)/n$. This binary coding is justified only
because the question contrasts the two retained source relations. Collapsing a
genuinely three-way lemma question to one versus other would answer a different
question.

```{r}
#| label: plot-ud-categorical
#| fig-cap: "Empirical mass functions for interrogative lemma and annotated dependency relation in the Turkish BOUN extract."
plot_data <- rbind(
  data.frame(variable = "Interrogative lemma", category = lemma_counts$lemma,
             probability = lemma_counts$probability),
  data.frame(variable = "Dependency relation", category = relation_counts$relation,
             probability = relation_counts$probability)
)

ggplot(plot_data, aes(category, probability)) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey45", width = 0.72) +
  facet_wrap(~variable, scales = "free_x", ncol = 1) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Empirical probability") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The categorical model preserves which lemma occurred; the Bernoulli mapping collapses the relation to a success/failure indicator. That collapse is useful only when the binary property answers the linguistic question.

## Check your understanding

1. Recompute the categorical PMF for `dependency_relation` directly from `questions`.
2. Define a Bernoulli indicator for lemma *ne* and compute its empirical $p$.
3. Explain why treating the `object` indicator as a Bernoulli variable does not make the rows independent.
4. Which information is lost when `dependency_relation` replaces the three-level lemma?
5. A student codes *ne* as one and every other lemma as zero, then calls the
   result the lemma distribution. Which information has been collapsed?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The empirical relation PMF is $p_R(\text{nsubj})=51/167=0.305389$ and $p_R(\text{obj})=116/167=0.694611$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. For $I_{\textit{ne}}=\mathbb{1}\{L=\textit{ne}\}$, the empirical Bernoulli parameter is $p=147/167=0.880240$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. Bernoulli coding specifies two possible row values but does not make rows independent, because multiple tokens can come from the same sentence and register. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. Replacing the three-level lemma with dependency relation discards which of *hangi*, *kim*, or *ne* the token instantiates. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
5. The binary variable preserves only *ne* versus non-*ne* and can no longer
   distinguish *hangi* from *kim*.

</details>

A categorical variable retains one of $K$ labels, whereas a Bernoulli variable
retains the answer to one binary question. Under the stated row weighting, the
MLE in either case is an empirical relative frequency. The [next
page](bernoulli-distribution.qmd) develops the Bernoulli expectation and
variance.
